statement: A game piece starts on the bottom-left square of a $3 \times 3$ board and must reach the top-right square. Each move takes it one square to the right, one square up, or one square diagonally up and to the right. In how many different ways can it get there?

choices.misconception: I only counted routes made of right and up moves, 4!/(2! 2!) = 6, and forgot the diagonal moves.
I counted the 6 right-and-up routes plus the route of two diagonal moves, but forgot routes that use one diagonal move.
I counted 3 places for the diagonal in routes with one diagonal move, but always put right before up, so I got 6 + 3 + 1 = 10.
I counted 6 routes with no diagonal and 6 routes with one diagonal, but forgot the route made of two diagonal moves.

hints: Sort the routes by how many diagonal moves they use: $0$, $1$ or $2$.
The piece must go $2$ squares right and $2$ squares up in total. A diagonal move does one of each at once.
No diagonal: arrange R, R, U, U in $6$ ways. One diagonal: arrange D, R, U in $3! = 6$ ways. Two diagonals: $1$ way. Add.

solutions.reliable: The piece must go $2$ squares right and $2$ squares up in all. If it uses no diagonal moves, it makes the moves R, R, U, U in some order: $\frac{4!}{2!\,2!} = 6$ ways. If it uses one diagonal move D, the other moves are one R and one U, and the three different moves can be ordered in $3! = 6$ ways. If it uses two diagonal moves, there is $1$ way. In all, $6 + 6 + 1 = 13$.
solutions.elegant: Write the number of ways to reach each square. Every square gets the sum of the counts from the square to its left, the square below it and the square diagonally below-left. The bottom row and left column are all $1$; the middle square gets $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$; the squares next to the top-right corner get $1 + 3 + 1 = 5$; the top-right square gets $5 + 5 + 3 = 13$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
